newsitem.title: UK: Bradys' days are numbered as market demise begins.
newsitem.headline: Bradys' days are numbered as market demise begins.

text.p: With the Philippines and Mexico sponging away the stigma of default by retiring their outstanding U.S.-Brady bonds, analysts are starting to predict the imminent demise of the $1,600 billion market.

Mexico amazed international financiers in May when it issued a $1.75 billion global bond with a 30-year maturity, and used the proceeds to retire $1.24 billion of its Brady bonds, issued by developing countries to reduce outstanding debts and guaranteed by the U.S. treasury.
The Philippines has already followed its lead while Brazil, Peru, Argentina and Venezuela are eager to tread the same path.
"I think we're going to see this as a growing trend," said Ousmene Mandeng, fixed income strategist at West Merchant Bank in London.

"The Brady market is going to merge into the larger class of bonds outstanding. It's a natural process that started with the huge amount of Eurobond issuance since 1993, mainly from Latin America," he added.
"I very much believe it will become one market, probably within a year, as spreads contract."
Mandeng is not alone in predicting the end of the Brady market -- at least in its current form.

Nicholas Brady, the former U.S. Treasury Secretary who masterminded the 1989 debt reduction plan that fathered the Brady market, himself said 10 days ago he could foresee the demise of the market that bears his name.
"I hope all the Bradys go through the process, where the country stands on its own two feet," he told London financiers in the light of the Mexican move. "It's a sign of progress."
Last month the Philippines issued nearly $700 million in 20-year Eurobonds and swapped them for its Brady debt, foreign commercial loans formed into bonds after the 1980s debt crisis.
Analysts are still awed by Mexico's feat in launching so long-dated an issue of pure Mexican risk less than 18 months after a peso devaluation sparked a major financial crisis.
Inspired by their success, Peru two weeks ago said it too would buy back some of its Bradys -- though the market suspects it had already taken that step well before the announcement.
Now Brazil has passed legislation so it too can follow suit, while traders bet whether Argentina or Venezuela will be next.
The trend towards retiring Brady debt will probably result in the merger of existing debt markets, with Brady bonds traded together with Eurobonds, and at comparable spreads.

Yield spreads between Brady bonds, and fresh debt Brady nations have issued on the Eurobond market, have already begun to converge as their economies strengthen and return-hungry investors feel confident with exposure to pure country risk.

Researchers at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell noted last week that the staggering growth in Latin America's foreign reserves, now $110 billion, was fast approaching the $122 billion total of the region's outstanding Brady debt, leaving these countries well positioned to buy back their high yielding obligations.
Doing so means that the Brady nations can shed the stigma of past default, lengthen the tenor of their outstanding debt, or replace it with cheaper paper launched on the Eurobond market.

It also frees up the U.S. dollar component that serves as collateral within particular Brady instruments, the so-called Par and Discount bonds issued by Argentina, Bulgaria, Brazil, Ecuador, Mexico, Panama, Poland and Venezuela.

The natural amortisation of such debt instruments may also play a part in the market's demise, while new reschedulings, like that Russia and the Ivory Coast are negotiating with their commercial creditors, will not add new Bradys the market.

The instruments born of such talks will be Brady-style rather than Brady bonds proper since they involve no debt relief. The Ivory Coast is seen as the last significant debtor to agree such a deal, with around $3 billion under negotiation.
